title: Frappe Accounting
body:
ERPNext Accounting
features & workflow

A practical reference for business teams: documents, money movements, ledger entries, financial reports and controls.

FEATURE TREE / WORKFLOW TREE / WORKED EXAMPLE
Prepared for Judibas product discussion

Research checked: 21 October 2026
Includes a separate Frappe Books overview

Independent guide based on official public documentation. No private ERPNext or Frappe Books account was inspected. Product behaviour depends on the installed version, permissions and configuration.

title: 01 / Scope and product names
body:
ERPNext Accounting is the main subject of this guide. It connects financial records to business documents and their ledger effects. Frappe Books is a separate accounting product; it is summarized on page 16. Do not assume the two products share every screen or feature. [1, 16]

PagesWhat you will find
3-4Feature tree and accounting workflow tree
5-8Setup, sales, purchases, payments and banking
9-12Journals, budgets, reports, permissions and audit
13Complete service-business accounting example
14-15Related workflows, rollout checklist and glossary
16-17Frappe Books overview and official sources

The basic idea

An operational document describes the business event. Submitting an accounting document creates its ledger effect. Receiving or paying money is a separate event from issuing an invoice. Reports summarize the resulting records. [1, 13]

Labels: [D] documented ERPNext behaviour. [C] dependent on setup, related modules or version. [E] illustrative example or recommended practice. This is an overview for understanding and scoping, not an exhaustive field-by-field implementation manual.

Sources: [1] ERPNext accounting introduction, [13] Accounting entries, [16] Frappe Books product overview

title: 03 / Accounting workflow tree
body:
How a business event becomes a posted accounting record, is settled, and appears in management reports.

Document and ledger flow: [3-7, 12-13]. Review and recovery activities in step 7 include recommended operating practices [E].

title: 04 / Company and account setup
body:
Chart of accounts [D]

The chart is a hierarchy for assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses. Group accounts organize the tree; actual postings use ledger accounts. Account type, company and currency influence how accounts can be used. [2]

Account familyPlain-language purposeExample [E]
AssetsResources controlled by the businessBank, cash, receivables
LiabilitiesAmounts owedSupplier payables, accrued costs
EquityOwner interest and retained resultsCapital, retained earnings
IncomeRevenue earnedConsulting revenue
ExpensesCosts incurredRent, utilities

Recommended setup order [E]

  • Confirm company identity, reporting currency and fiscal dates.
  • Agree the account structure and default receivable/payable accounts.
  • Prepare customer, supplier, item and bank details.
  • Configure relevant taxes, payment terms and cost centers.
  • Choose one migration cutoff and reconcile opening balances.
  • Test draft and submitted transactions before wider rollout.
Company setup defines the accounting entity. A department or project reporting tag does not create another legal company. Avoid building a separate account for every department when a dimension can represent that distinction. [8]

Sources: [2] Chart of accounts, [8] Accounting dimensions

title: 05 / Sales and customer collection
body:
Sales Invoice [D]

A Sales Invoice records the customer obligation, income and applicable taxes when submitted. It can follow a Sales Order or Delivery Note, or be entered directly. Item income accounts, payment terms and reporting dimensions must be correct. Stock updating is a separate choice that must match the delivery workflow. [3]

StepBusiness purposeCheck [E]
Prepare invoiceDefine customer, goods/services and amountCompany, currency, dates and item rates
Review and submitPost the invoice accounting effectIncome account, tax and due date
Record receiptRecognize money receivedBank/cash account and reference
Allocate paymentConnect receipt to invoiceCorrect invoice and allocation amount
Follow upCollect the remaining balanceReceivables and overdue balances

Partial payment example [E]

Invoice the customer Rs 100,000 and receive Rs 60,000. If that receipt is allocated to the invoice, Rs 40,000 remains outstanding. The receipt is not a second sale. Multiple payments can settle one invoice, and a payment may cover several invoices. [5]

A draft invoice is not the same as a submitted invoice. A submitted invoice is not proof of payment. Keep document status, accounting posting and cash collection distinct.

Sources: [3] Sales invoice, [5] Payment entry

title: 06 / Purchases and supplier balances
body:
Purchase Invoice [D]

A Purchase Invoice records a supplier bill and, on submission, its payable and related expense, asset value or other account effects. It may be based on a Purchase Order or Purchase Receipt, or entered directly. Review supplier references and posting dates. [4]

ScenarioTypical routeKey distinction
Service bought on creditPurchase Invoice, then Payment EntryExpense and payment happen separately
Goods already receivedInvoice from the existing Purchase ReceiptAvoid recording receipt twice
Goods and bill togetherInvoice with stock update where appropriateRequires the intended stock configuration
Supplier paid in advanceAdvance Payment Entry and later allocationPayment may precede the final invoice

Unpaid supplier example [E]

A service bill is Rs 30,000. After a payment of Rs 20,000 is allocated, Rs 10,000 remains payable. The bill still records a Rs 30,000 obligation; the payment settles part of it. [5]

Recommended check [E]: confirm whether stock was already received through another voucher before enabling invoice stock updates. Check duplicate supplier invoice references before submission.

Sources: [4] Purchase invoice, [5] Payment entry, [14] Inventory accounting

title: 07 / Payments, allocation and banking
body:
Payment Entry [D]

Payment Entry supports Receive, Pay and Internal Transfer. It records account movements, parties, references and allocations. Advances may remain unallocated until matched later. [5]

ToolPurposeWhat it does not prove
Payment EntryRecord money received, paid or transferredAn unallocated receipt does not settle a specific invoice
Payment ReconciliationAllocate existing payments/credits to invoicesIt does not compare your books with a bank statement
Bank ReconciliationMatch statement lines with recorded vouchersAn imported statement line is not automatically a new sale
Internal TransferMove money between company accountsIt is not additional business income

Bank reconciliation [D]

Select the company bank account and date range, import or synchronize transactions through supported methods, and match statement activity to existing vouchers. Check for an existing record before creating a missing one. Record fees and explain timing differences. Verify the ending balance against the statement. [7]

A cheque reference is a payment reference, not a complete cheque-management lifecycle. Issued, held, deposited, cleared, returned and replaced cheque states need a separately agreed workflow [E]. Bank-provider support must also be verified for the chosen country and installation [C].

Sources: [5] Payment entry, [7] Bank reconciliation

title: 08 / Journals and ledger protection
body:
Journal Entry [D]

A Journal Entry records balanced debits and credits directly. It is suitable for adjustments, accruals, opening balances, write-offs and revaluations. Normal customer receipts and supplier payments are generally clearer through Payment Entry because it handles party and invoice allocations explicitly. [6]

Illustrative event [E]DebitCredit
Recognize unpaid electricity Rs 8,000Utilities expense 8,000Accrued liability 8,000
Owner deposits Rs 50,000Bank 50,000Owner capital 50,000
Expense prepaid for future periodPrepaid expenseBank

Corrections and cancellation [D]

ERPNext's immutable-ledger design preserves original postings and records reversals on cancellation. Corrections should follow the supported document process rather than manually overwriting ledger rows. Backdated accounting or stock changes can affect later values and require careful diagnosis. [12]

Recommended control [E]: restrict journal and cancellation permissions, require a clear explanation and retain supporting evidence. A balanced journal can still use the wrong accounts, party or reporting period.

Sources: [6] Journal entry, [12] Immutable ledger

title: 09 / Dimensions, budgets and books
body:
Accounting dimensions [D]

An account describes what occurred; a dimension describes the business segment. ERPNext treats Cost Center and Project as dimensions and supports configurable additional dimensions, such as Department. Required dimensions affect submission and should be tested across invoices, payments and journals. [8]

Example [E]AccountReporting tag
Marketing campaignAdvertising expenseDepartment = Marketing
Client implementationService revenueProject = Client Portal
Office rentRent expenseCost Center = Head Office

Budgets [D / C]

Budgets compare planned account amounts against activity for a configured segment and period. Warning or blocking depends on the selected transaction stages and control settings. Matching company, dates, account and dimension values matters. [9]

Finance Book [D / C]

Finance Books support alternate accounting treatments or report views within the same company. Use one only when that requirement exists; it is not a replacement for separate companies or department tagging. Keep the selected book explicit when comparing results. [15]

Recommended design [E]: begin with a clean account tree and a small number of useful dimensions. Add complexity only where it answers a real reporting or control requirement.

Sources: [8] Accounting dimensions, [9] Budgets, [15] Finance books

title: 10 / Reports and management decisions
body:
Accounting reports present posted transactions from different perspectives. Choose the report according to the question, then trace unusual figures to source vouchers. [10, 18]

ReportQuestion answered
General LedgerWhich debit/credit entries produced this balance?
Trial BalanceWhat are opening, movement and closing balances by account?
Balance SheetWhat does the company own and owe on a date?
Profit and LossWhat income and expenses produced the period result?
Cash FlowWhy did cash change across business activities?
Accounts ReceivableWhich customer invoices remain unpaid or overdue?
Accounts PayableWhich supplier amounts remain due?
Payment LedgerHow do invoice/payment allocations explain outstanding balances?

Reading sequence [E]

  • Start with the financial statement or outstanding-balance report.
  • Confirm company, date range, currency and any dimension or Finance Book filters.
  • Open detailed ledger activity for an unexpected account or party.
  • Open the original submitted voucher and review its allocations.
A trial balance that balances is not proof that every transaction is correct. An incorrect expense classification can leave debits and credits perfectly equal [E].

Sources: [10] Accounting reports, [18] General ledger

title: 11 / Roles, approvals and audit
body:
Permission model [D]

Roles grant access to document types and actions such as reading, writing and submitting. Additional user restrictions and field permission levels can narrow access. A job title alone should not determine unrestricted financial access. [11]

Suggested responsibility [E]Typical access to consider
Accounts operatorPrepare invoices and payments within assigned company scope
AccountantReview postings, reconcile accounts and prepare adjustments
Accounts managerAuthorize sensitive accounting actions and oversight
Business managerRead permitted reports and relevant business documents
System administratorMaintain the application; grant financial powers explicitly
Employee / customerOnly the documents and portal workflows relevant to them

Document controls [E]

  • Separate preparation, approval and payment responsibilities where practical.
  • Test read, submit, cancel, amend, export and cross-company access.
  • Require clear references and evidence for sensitive changes.
  • Use supported reversal/correction processes and review period boundaries.
  • Test backup restoration; an export alone is not a complete recovery plan.
The responsibility matrix is a proposed operating policy. It is not a claim that these exact restrictions or approval stages are enabled by default. Configure and verify them in the chosen ERPNext version.

Sources: [11] Role-based permissions, [12] Immutable ledger

title: 12 / Complete accounting example
body:
Original service-business illustration [E]: one currency, no tax, no stock, no opening balances and no other activity. Amounts are in rupees.

Business eventDocumentIllustrative posting
Bill customer Rs 100,000Submitted Sales InvoiceDebit receivables 100,000; credit revenue 100,000
Receive Rs 60,000Allocated Receive Payment EntryDebit bank 60,000; credit receivables 60,000
Supplier service bill Rs 30,000Submitted Purchase InvoiceDebit expense 30,000; credit payables 30,000
Pay supplier Rs 20,000Allocated Pay Payment EntryDebit payables 20,000; credit bank 20,000

What the reports should explain

MeasureAmountInterpretation
RevenueRs 100,000Earned amount in this illustration
ExpenseRs 30,000Cost incurred
ProfitRs 70,000Revenue minus expense
Net bank movementRs 40,000 increase60,000 received minus 20,000 paid
Customer receivableRs 40,000Still to collect
Supplier payableRs 10,000Still to pay
Profit is not cash received. Payments change settlement and bank balances; they do not create another invoice. Exact account names and postings depend on configuration. This is an explanation of accounting logic, not a local tax calculation.

Sources: [13] Accounting entries, [3] Sales invoice, [4] Purchase invoice, [5] Payment entry

title: 13 / Links with other business modules
body:
Stock and inventory [D / C]

Stock movements can connect to financial entries under perpetual inventory. Delivery, receipt and invoice flows must be designed together so that stock is not updated twice. Review stock account mappings and reconcile stock-related ledger values using the supported reports. [14]

Related areaRelationship to accountingScope decision [E]
Sales / CRMA commercial opportunity can lead to an order and invoiceDecide the handover point from CRM
Purchasing / inventoryReceipts and supplier bills explain goods and obligationsChoose receipt versus invoice stock updating
AssetsAsset acquisition and subsequent accounting have specialized workflowsConfirm the asset module and policy
ProjectsProject tags segment revenue and costsDefine shared project identifiers
HR / payrollPayroll or claims can produce financial obligationsConfirm the installed HR/payroll apps
Cheque managementReferences and clearance relate to paymentsDefine the full cheque lifecycle separately

For Judibas planning [E]

Use this as a functional reference. A similar feature list does not migrate ERPNext's accounting engine into Laravel. Reusing ERPNext through integration versus implementing a Judibas-native ledger are different projects, with different data ownership, testing and maintenance requirements.

Sources: [1] ERPNext accounting introduction, [8] Accounting dimensions, [14] Inventory accounting

title: 14 / Rollout checklist and glossary
body:
Recommended acceptance checks [E]

  • Opening balances and unpaid invoices match the agreed migration cutoff.
  • Invoice submission, partial payment and allocation produce expected balances.
  • Supplier bills, advances and final payments reconcile correctly.
  • Cancellation retains traceable original and reversal records.
  • Bank matching does not create duplicate transactions.
  • Reports agree under consistent company, period and dimension filters.
  • Unassigned users cannot read, modify or export another company's financial records.
  • Large exports, backups and simultaneous users are tested before launch.

Plain-language glossary

TermMeaning
Ledger accountPosting account used to classify financial effects.
VoucherSource accounting document linked to ledger activity.
Receivable / payableAmount to collect / amount owed.
AllocationLink between payment amount and an invoice or reference.
Cost center / dimensionBusiness segment used for analysis or control.
JournalDeliberate balanced debit/credit entry.
ReversalOpposite posting preserving the original transaction trail.
ReconciliationExplaining differences between records and supporting evidence.

Sources: [2] Chart of accounts, [5] Payment entry, [6] Journal entry, [7] Bank reconciliation, [12] Immutable ledger

title: 15 / Frappe Books: separate product
body:
Current product scope [D]

The official Frappe Books site now describes a Frappe Framework application that teams can use in a browser on their own server, including from a phone. It states that the old desktop application is no longer supported. Older comparisons describing Books only as desktop software should therefore not be used for current product decisions. [16]

The product overview lists quotes, invoices, payments, supplier bills and returns; inventory and point of sale; double-entry accounting; and reports including Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, General Ledger and Trial Balance. It also describes team permissions. [16]

How to evaluate it separately [E]

QuestionWhat to inspect
Is the workflow simple enough for your team?Try sales, purchasing and payment allocation with sample records.
Does it meet local requirements?Verify relevant taxes, printed documents and any required local integrations.
Does it cover the controls you need?Test permissions, corrections, reporting and recovery.
Does it fit the wider suite?Compare actual integration needs against ERPNext and Judibas.

Its report documentation describes filtered report tables, exports and links back to underlying documents. Confirm the exact installed release before documenting a production workflow. [17]

The ERPNext feature and workflow trees in this guide describe ERPNext Accounting. They are not a promise that Frappe Books implements every ERPNext dimension, budget, permission or operational feature.

Sources: [16] Frappe Books product overview, [17] Frappe Books reports
